what_it_does: FPGAs (field-programmable gate arrays — chips whose internal logic can be reconfigured by software after manufacture) are controlled by configuration memory: tiny cells that store bits saying which logic blocks are connected and how. Traditionally, those memory cells are built from silicon SRAM (static RAM — six transistors per bit, fast but bulky), and they consume a large fraction of the chip's area. This paper proposes moving the configuration memory out of the main silicon layer and into the 'back-end-of-line' (BEOL) — the stack of metal wiring layers built on top of the silicon that normally just carries signals. The BEOL memory is made from amorphous oxide semiconductor (AOS) transistors, which are thin-film devices that can be deposited on top of existing circuitry at relatively low temperature. Because the configuration cells now sit physically above the logic they control rather than beside it, routing distances shrink and the silicon area freed up can be used for more logic, potentially making the FPGA denser and faster.
